utterances.text: Of course I'm referring to a specific area since I only visited a specific rural area. I can't make broader generalisations. If you want my opinion, it's probably the case the areas of Southern Kosovo were more deeply affected by these operations than other areas, but I can only speak about the areas that I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Drenica. Do you know that this area of Drenica, this triangle of Drenica, was the focal point of the terrorist organisation of the KLA there?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that's what's claimed. I do not believe that that is a justification for the extensive indiscriminate actions taken by your forces in pursuit of those terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that in this area of Drenica, after the Second World War, for seven years the army was chasing gangs of these broken units that had served in Hitler's army during the Second World War? They were still hiding in the hills of Drenica seven years after the end of the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is that this is a hotbed of destabilisation. It had been that for a long time. A source of banditism, looting, and even during the two world wars the Royal Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll put that to the witness to see if he knows. Lord Ashdown, do you know that this was a hotbed of banditry, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it was so claimed, and I have no reason to doubt that. I also know that in this area some appalling crimes were committed against Albanians, including the dreadful massacre of family while I was there - I didn't see it so I haven't given evidence of it - in which they were not only massacred as a family, men, women, and children, the elderly and the young, and appalling mutilated in the process. I cannot give evidence of that because I didn't see it myself, though no doubt others can. None of this alters my evidence, which was that in tackling, as they were legitimately entitled to do, the issue of terrorism and disorder in their country, Mr. Milosevic forces used means which were excessive, indiscriminate, designed to drive out the civilian population and, as I would say, illegal under international law. And I believe that it is also relevant that Mr. Milosevic was informed of this at our meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You told us about that. Just one moment. Mr. Milosevic, you remember that you finish at half past three. You have not yet asked any questions about the meeting. If you wish to ask any questions about the meeting, if you dispute any of the witness's evidence about the meeting, you should do so in the time that is allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, but of course. But please bear in mind that the witness has been taking up most of the time. It would be very easy if time were spent by me receiving answers to my questions. Does he know things or does he not know things? Every time invariably the witness makes a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would say it's six of one and a half dozen of the other. But let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned killings, et cetera, awhile ago. Are you aware of the fact that this same police that you have been ascribing killings to, even during the chaos of war, arrested several hundreds of Yugoslav citizens because of killings, rapes, lootings, et cetera, precisely in order to prevent and punish these killings? Are you aware of that? Are you aware that there was an order by the Supreme Command for every such illegal activity and perpetrated crime to be punished rigorously, to have the perpetrators arrested immediately, and brought before legal institutions? Do you know anything about that or do you not know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because you informed me that that's what would happen. I also know that on many occasions you said things would happen which never did happen, including that the operations to which I have referred would stop, I think, two days before we observed them going on. Mr. Milosevic, I'm afraid there was a considerable gap, well-identified by many, between what you personally and your government said and what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that I was somewhat better informed than you, but let me move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to Decani, did you visit any other Serb monasteries or churches? Just say yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you well know from my evidence, I didn't have time to do so, but I made certain that I did visit Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Have you heard of -- of at least one event or several events that a Serb monastery or a church or an Orthodox cemetery were targets of terrorist attacks?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I not only know that, I've seen the photographs presented to me by Serb authorities, at least afterwards, of incidents where that happened. I didn't in any way seek to indicate by visiting Decani and finding it in pristine condition that that applied to any other Serb religious site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, that only from the arrival of KFOR and UNMIK there, 108 Serb churches were demolished in Kosovo under the patronage of the KFOR? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I indeed know that that has occurred since the necessity of NATO intervention because you wouldn't heed the warnings. I have publicly condemned those, but I don't see what relevance that has to the issues on which I'm giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In relation to the question that you brought me, the question of Prime Minister -- the letter of Prime Minister Blair, I assume it is clear that the point of our meeting was to have Prime Minister Blair's letter delivered.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The point of our meeting was, by the by, to have Prime Minister Blair's letter to be delivered. I undertook to perform that service for him, as you well know. But the point of our meeting was for me to give you my impressions of what was going on and, in the light of the conclusions I reached, to warn you, specifically and in perhaps blunter terms than was in Prime Minister Blair's letter, that you should not underestimate the determination of the international community to uphold international law; that if you continued to operate grossly and flagrantly in contravention to that law, that intervention would inevitably be followed and that you were personally indictable for any instance of that that occurred that you knew about, and you did know about them after my visit. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've already said that several times, so let's save time, if possible. Is it clear, therefore, that I received you because you were an envoy of the Prime Minister of Great Britain and since you were bringing his letter?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you received me, Mr. Milosevic. I was grateful to you that you did. But I don't think you could have been in any doubt at the end of that meeting what the purpose of that meeting was, and it was for me to tell you my impressions and to give you those warnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We read the letter. You gave it out here as well, this concern, et cetera. However, do you remember that the core of the matter was the comment on what Prime Minister Blair had said, that he wished to join in the efforts to find a peaceful solution, and that that was the core of the matter, as far as both sides were concerned, the wish and the idea -- the key word, so to speak - how shall I put this? - was a peaceful solution?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blair must account for the meaning of his letter, but I would have thought you knew that very clearly from the text of the letter. My purpose was to give you my impressions and to make the warnings that I made. I delivered the letter to you from Mr. Blair. This is his letter, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was a letter that you brought, that I read in front of you, and it must have been a subject of our comments. So I'm asking you now: Since that was underway then, precisely this quest for a peaceful solution, do you remember what I said to you what I considered to be the key: that we are proposing - and that was already written in these documents - for a peaceful solution? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, Mr. Milosevic, I cannot remember you saying those words, but I don't exclude that possibility, since I was also in favour of a peaceful solution. But I warned you that such a peaceful solution could not happen if you continued with the actions that I had just seen, and you would then, by your actions, make NATO intervention absolutely inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown, let me just remind you: Since this was a very simple formula that we had been offering, I told you - and of course the Americans knew that as well, those who were talking to us about this, and all the rest who were involved - that a political solution had to be found based on the principle of equality of citizens and equality of ethnic communities, that is to say, both one and the other, and that therefore we proposed this. And we agreed on all points except that from our point of view there were some unprincipled reservations, that this equality of citizens and equality of the national minorities in Kosovo should be expressed in such a way that the parliament of Kosovo would have two Chambers. One would be the Chamber of Citizens that would be elected according to the principle "one man, one vote," and the second one would be the Chamber of Ethnic Communities, in which every ethnic community would delegate on the basis of parity and number of its own delegates. That was the essence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I do because, as you've seen from my report, I recommend that those negotiations towards a peaceful solution should be continued. You've seen that very clearly from my evidence. But I warned you that you would destroy these chances for a peaceful solution if you continued in the use of excessive force, contrary to international law, and that you would then bring about the necessity of a NATO intervention and involve yourself, as well, in the possibility of indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to skip a few questions in order to abide by this time limit, although I don't think I can fit into this remaining half hour or so. In writing here, and in this written statement that you gave and also during your testimony here, you said several times -- or rather, you referred to the Geneva Convention several times and the Second Protocol. First of all, is it clear that the Geneva Convention relates to war conflicts between states?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may read you the Second Protocol -- and I have to say to you, Mr. Milosevic, you're a lawyer, I'm not, so I must leave the judgement of these matters to this Court. But I'm happy to leave you to -- to give you, if you haven't got it, or to read out the specific items of Protocol II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be, Lord Ashdown, most helpful if we dealt with what was said at the meeting rather than in generalities, which we appear to have been doing so far. What was the reference at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference at the meeting, as I remember it, Your Honour, was exactly that given in my testimony, which referred to the item which we introduced as evidence. It was paragraph 8(d) of the founding Statutes of the International Court. I haven't got the document with me here, but I can read it again if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We now have that document. Can I distribute that? It's rather more substantial than the copy that Lord Ashdown has entered this morning, and I haven't, of course, been able to check how many pages he has, but here it comes in full. So as not to interrupt you further --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me, please, to have these things clarified first. Of course, this can be handed out. Anything can be handed out. But I keep looking at the time, and you're limiting my time. Let us clarify one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that the Geneva Convention relates to conflicts between states, not internal conflicts, and the fact that in the Second Protocol there are provisions that are related to internal conflicts, and because here this is mentioned a great deal, I would like you to bear in mind paragraph 2.1 of the Second Protocol, which says quite clearly: [In English] "This Protocol shall not apply to situations of internal disturbances and tensions, such as riots, isolated and sporadic acts of violence and other acts of similar nature, as not being armed conflicts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, none of this has to do with the witness's evidence. You can make these points to us in due course, as a matter of law, of course, but the witness's evidence has nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, it has a great deal to do with it, because the witness, a countless number of times, pointed this out, and the rest that is stipulated here is even clearer. It's one minute. So please allow me to clarify this. Article 3 reads: [In English] "Nothing in this protocol shall be invoked for the purpose of affecting the sovereignty of a State or the responsibility of the government, by all legitimate means, to maintain or re-establish law and order in the State or to defend the national unity and the territorial integrity of the State." [Interpretation] And the next paragraph says -- let me just finish: [In English] "Nothing in this Protocol shall be invoked as a justification for intervening, directly or indirectly, for any reason whatsoever, in the armed conflict or in the internal or external affairs of the High Contracting Party in the territory of which the conflict occurs." [Interpretation] Therefore, this protocol -- well, please, let me put a question, because I've read this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've allowed you to read this, but it is totally irrelevant. This is purely a matter of law. You can address us on it in due course. In any event, the witness was referring to a different document, which you can have now in front of you. If you want to ask him some question about what was said at the meeting, of course you can, but there's no point wasting time on matters of law at this stage. There will be a stage in which you can address us on it. Now, have you a further question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is important, because the witness pointed out the Second Protocol, and I've read the Second Protocol to you, and it says something that is quite contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us ask Lord Ashdown that. Just a moment. Did you refer to the Second Protocol, Lord Ashdown, in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As I made clear in my statement, and I've sought to assure myself of the document that I left with Mr. Milosevic, it was not, indeed, the Second Protocol, though I note in passing -- and again this is -- I'm not able to comment on the legalities. Mr. Milosevic's quotation carefully do not include Article 1 of part I, which I think defines this conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is exactly why we should not be getting into this argument now. It's a question of law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But may I just help the Court in this sense, Your Honour, that the document that I left with or referred to Mr. Milosevic is not part II. It is, indeed, the Statutes of the International Criminal Court, and if I recall, the International Court had established that a conflict existed in Kosovo prior to my visit in the terms of that Statute, and the reference I made to Mr. Milosevic was the one that I quoted, Article 8, which says this: "For the purposes of the Statute, war crimes in a conflict ..." It doesn't say -- but "'war crimes' means grave breaches of the Geneva Convention, namely, any of the following acts against persons or property protected under the provisions of the relevant Geneva Convention." And then it lists as subpara 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. It is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. It lists, under paragraph 4, "Extensive destruction and appropriation of property not justified by military necessity and carried out unlawfully and wantonly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is significant is more the fact of your having referred Mr. Milosevic to that document than any particular legal interpretation of it, because the legal interpretation is not a question that we are going to deal with at this time. And I think we'll only waste time if we continue to delve into that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, awhile ago the witness said he had not mentioned the Second Protocol. In the text of his statement it says: "The excessive use of force, which is in contravention of the Geneva Convention from 1977 and the Second Protocol." That's what it says here in the written statement, in his written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. You pointed that -- you have pointed that out, and it's been pointed out to you what the relevance of all this is for this part of the trial. Now, if you have any questions about -- about this matter, about what the witness said to you, you should put it to him rather than trying to argue matters of law now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is relevant, because one has to point out the legal nature of the conflict. The conflict between the legitimate and legal authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are ruling it is irrelevant for this witness, and it is pointless to go on arguing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think you should switch off my microphone during the cross-examination, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It will be switched off if you go on asking irrelevant questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, as for crimes and internal conflicts, it is that Second Protocol, Article 6, which indicates the authorities of the national courts which we in fact did do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have an explanation, for example, for the events that are taking place in Macedonia, that the Macedonian army is using planes, helicopters, heavy artillery, tanks, against Albanian terrorists and nobody has characterised that conflict as a war conflict or anybody threatened them with any bombing or aggression?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not relevant to the witness's evidence. I notice that you haven't challenged anything that was said at the meeting. So we can therefore assume that it's not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On that topic, Your Honour, may I -- on that topic, the fuller extract from the diary is now available. I promised it would be. It could be distributed usefully at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. What the Prosecution is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just quickly deal with this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The ICC Statute will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit 79, and the diary Prosecution Exhibit 80.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution cannot interrupt my cross-examination, Mr. May. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As -- according to what I have on page 8 of your statement of the 18th of October, 2000, paragraph 8.3, you present your views about the independence of Kosovo as a long-term objective. And 5.1 and 5.2, you advocate the use of air force against the army in Kosovo, airstrikes. My question is the following --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise if I'm taking up more time. I need to know precisely what document he's referring to here.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the report on the visit to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I can't find my way in these heaps of paper, but you can check it out later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's the -- the witness statement for the Tribunal, 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. The 18th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got that, Lord Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't immediately lay my hands on it, Your Honour, I fear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a copy coming up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to lose time, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but just tell the witness where you're reading from so he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 8 of the statement of the 18th of October, 2000, 8.3 paragraph, the "Independence of Kosovo as a long-term objective," and paragraphs 5.1 and 5.2, "Advocating Airstrikes in Kosovo against the Yugoslav army."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. The document -- perhaps the clerk could help me towards where there is, because I don't have a page 8 here. I don't wish to take up the time of the Court, but I simply do not have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the document is that headed "Report on Visit" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- "to Kosovo" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- "26th to 29th of September."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excellent. I have that. Mr. Milosevic, could you direct me to where you are referring on that document, which presumably is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, you knew your position, that you strove for the bombing of Yugoslavia. You advocated that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, Mr. Milosevic, as you know well. I told you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said no. You say no.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interview with you, Mr. Milosevic, was to warn you that if you continued, the intervention of NATO was inevitable. I sought to avoid that intervention. That was the purpose of our interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you said about the NATO intervention that it was legal and was not in contravention to the United Nations Charter a moment ago when I asked you about that today here.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was commenting on an opinion about an event that happened well after this. Your contention that I came to you proposing the use of bombing against Kosovo is completely incorrect. That was neither the purpose of my meeting nor was it the substance of my report. Indeed, I came to warn you to precisely avoid that outcome. I said to you, if you continued, that would be the inevitable outcome. I was trying to avoid it. What happened subsequently, the NATO intervention, was nothing to do with what I said, it was to do with what you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you saw what we did even several months after that meeting of yours, the meeting you had with me, from the quotation that I gave you quoting your own Foreign Minister, Robin Cook, and the other participants in that meeting. You did not answer my question, the question about your position and stand as to Kosovo's independence.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expressed a view that in the end, the long-term independence of Kosovo would probably be the outcome, but I expressed it in exactly the terms which are laid out in this report. But, Mr. Milosevic, my view about the outcome of the final status of Kosovo is nothing to do with the events that I saw on this trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you're talking about the independence of Kosovo, does that -- when you say that, do you have in mind the fact that after this indictment, the May 1999 one when the war was stopped, when G7, G8 sent Antisari and Chernomyrdin to Belgrade and after that the UN resolution that was adopted, that it guaranteed the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and that was a condition for the war to cease because agreement had been reached on that point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is well outside the evidence which the witness has given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him about the report, of course, but nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And perhaps it might help the Court and perhaps even Mr. Milosevic, who may not have read my words precisely, if I were to quote what I said. I did not recommend the independence of Kosovo. I said, "We should not exclude that possibility as a long-term aim, even if we cannot yet foresee circumstances in which it may be wise or safe to achieve it." Indeed, if I am right, that is precisely the basis of the final settlement of this dispute. No one has said what the long-term position of Kosovo will be, but it is not excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But don't you think that you cannot make a long-term status for Kosovo of any kind which would be contrary to the final settlement for the war which guaranteed the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that may or may not be a correct description of the outcome of this contest -- of this -- of this event, but the reality of it is that that was an opinion which I expressed to my government, and as I understand it, it remains the basic international position today. We have not yet resolved the long-term status of Kosovo, although I am bound to say that does not have any relevance to the evidence that I have given about these particular events on these particular days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you guarantee the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Yugoslavia, what do you -- it's not up to you to determine and resolve the status of Kosovo. Why should you do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a hypothetical question which has nothing to do with the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a hypothetical question, Mr. May, because I asked a question. I said, "In what capacity would -- ought they to resolve the status of Kosovo if you guarantee the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yugoslavia as a condition to the end of war and Resolution 1244 of the UN Security Council."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. I have to hurry up with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1992, you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina for the first time. Do you remember events from those days when a British television crew made a false film about an alleged concentration camp which was filmed from inside a warehouse and filmed through a barbed wire, from the inside outwards?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This refers to events in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where it was, but I do know that Mr. Ashdown, at that time, after those false, rigged pictures on British television, asked the British government to bomb the Bosnian Serbs. Was that right or not? Did you do that or did you not?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I recommended early international intervention in order to suppress this conflict and suppress the crimes being committed on both sides. And I'm bound to say, Mr. Milosevic, that if that recommendation had been followed, many tens of thousands of lives, including the lives, livelihoods, and homes, of many thousands of Serbs would have been saved. And if I may reflect that the consequences of your actions, both in that and in previous and subsequent actions, has led to a situation where there are three-quarters of a million Serbs who have lost their homes, many of their livelihoods, many of their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, but time is passing, and you have more or less used your time, used up your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness -- let the accused ask his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many lives would have been saved had the Vance-Owen Plan of 1993 have been accepted on the 1st of May in Athens, for example? And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are now getting a long way from the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You started off your testimony here with a menu of some kind from a dinner with Franjo Tudjman. I didn't understand very well what this has to do with this trial. And what do I care about your dinner with Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be a matter for the Trial Chamber to decide in due course, whether it's relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that was in 1995, already then. And I don't have to ask you that but that's what it says, in 1995. In 1995, in the autumn, the Dayton Agreement was signed. Therefore, even Tudjman at that time was clear as to which direction a solution would follow. So that I don't understand what it is that was the subject of your conversation or, to make things brief, what language did you talk in?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: English, if I recall. But, Mr. Milosevic, I've given my evidence on this, indeed I've -- the second court I've given it in. That evidence rests. I'm happy to answer any questions on it. I note, however, that you have not on any occasion refuted the details of the operations which I gave, which I witnessed on the 28th, 27th of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown -- Lord Ashdown, we must stop you. If you have further questions about the menu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question is linked to precisely that. That is to say that that alleged conversation with Tudjman at that time was used in the public as some sort of -- as the existence of some sort of agreement as to the division -- between Belgrade and Zagreb on the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which never existed. It was never an agreement and that that was a sort of justification for the crime that Croatia committed when in that same year it committed one of the greatest massacres and ethnic cleansing operations in the region of Krajina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember many speculating that that might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was rumoured and it was common knowledge that it was an operation which was covered by and in which the American company took part, NBRI, the American company NBRI, and mass crimes were committed against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question was: How could a conversation with Tudjman at a dinner, during a dinner, be used as alleged proof and evidence of the existence of an agreement of some kind about the division of Bosnia between Serbia and Croatia, especially when it was common knowledge that three years before that, prior to that, in 1992, when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are wasting time here. The witness cannot tell you what others made of the conversation. That is for the others to say. All he can give evidence about is the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'm quite clear. It's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the spring of 1999, during the NATO aggression, say publicly that you have evidence to show Serb war crimes committed in Kosovo? Because I saw here a film which shows you talking to a group of refugees in Kosovo. Is that the evidence and proof you were referring to, what we saw here?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The evidence -- I haven't seen this film and I do not know of its existence, but the evidence that I have of crimes contrary to international law is that that I have presented to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw that evidence, your conversation with a few women and children. We saw that.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the evidence that I presented this Court is the evidence in toto. It is the evidence of your guns, your artillery, your tanks bombarding from a distance of ten kilometres indiscriminately villages, driving out the civilian population, burning their houses, looting them. That's the evidence in toto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you saw in those two days; is that it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw over the period that I've given evidence before this Court, the evidence that I warned you about, and the evidence which supports the position which I said to you, if you continued, you would make it impossible for the international community not to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ashdown, is it customary for a leader of a small opposition party to visit, some ten times, a region in which there's a war going on, in some way on behalf of the government or in the name of the government? Is that customary, standard practice, in Great Britain?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's customary at all, and it's not what I did. I visited as the leader of a political party, on my own account, in order to inform myself of what is going on. I did not visit either as an envoy or on behalf of the British government, although in every case I thought it proper and right when I returned to provide for the Prime Minister of the time, whatever their party, a report on my findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, how did you come to carry a letter from the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this occasion, the Prime Minister knew. Indeed, it was public knowledge, Your Honour, that I was going out. He asked me to convey a letter for him. I acted as postman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether this could be interpreted perhaps as a double method, a dual method, in connection with the relationship towards Yugoslavia. Let me explain what I'm asking, in fact. I have here, for example, The Observer, dated May 2000, the 28th of May, which says the following: [In English] [As read] "[Previous translation continues] ... Balkan war military sale to Slovenia flouted Tory foreign policy. Britain flouted its own foreign policy by approving the sale of millions of pounds' worth of military equipment to former Yugoslavia, a republic, only days before the outbreak of the bloody Balkan war. [Indiscernible] has established eight days before Slovenia became the first area to break from unified Yugoslavia. In 1991 a British firm delivered," and so on, "equipment." [Interpretation] Does this in some way fit into the double methods that they have been writing about, that the British press has been referring to as well?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, perhaps it will help you -- I mean, I've always found you to be somebody who is rather well informed on British politics, but I think you seem to have somewhat misunderstood the situation. I was an opposition politician. Indeed, the fact that I raised the issues of Bosnia and of - particularly Bosnia, and later of Kosovo - was very unpopular at the time. I was shouted down in the House of Commons. The Prime Minister insulted me on several occasions. If what you are proposing is that somehow or another I was acting as an instrument of the British government, then I must only assume that you don't know about the politics of my country, because that is a laughable proposition, as any casual observer of those events would have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said, I think it was in The Guardian, in June of 1998, that the Balkans was quiet only when it was under the control of the big powers, the Ottoman Empire, the Austro-Hungarian and the Communists. I assume you remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's always been my view, unhappily. I hope we'll move to a different period in the Balkans in which each of the countries, as independent, peaceful neighbours, can establish the dominance of their own affairs through their own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Serbia rid itself of the Ottoman occupation as early on as the nineteenth century, that the uprising against the Turks was in 1804?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not as much of an expert in the history of your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. country as you, but I am aware of that broad historical thrust for your country. And so the point of this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point of the question is very clear, because if a politician, a British politician at that, who considers the fact that peace in the Balkans is possible only under the authority of the big powers and who, for example, is now a representative of the international community in Bosnia-Herzegovina becomes an international representative, does that mean consistency along the lines of the idea of an occupying presence, occupation presence, which in continuity has existed since the Austro-Hungarian Empire in the region, and does that indicate the idea -- indicate the motives to subjugate Yugoslavia, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, with the greatest respect, I've heard some fantastic theorising, some fantastic conspiracy theories from you, but this, I think, is the one that exceeds all others. Let me remind you that it is the apparently avowed intent of all of the previous Yugoslav countries, the ones that have left Yugoslavia under your government, to wish to join Europe, of their own free will. That provides precisely the kind of overarching structure which we in the European nations have enjoyed as an alternative to war. Now, surely that's what we would prefer to see. The idea that that is some great conspiracy of hegemony by Western powers to run other countries is, I think, so farfetched that I cannot even believe you believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, we're going to bring this political point to an end. You have a minute or two to put any more questions which are relevant to the indictment, not irrelevant ones.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few more questions, and I don't know why you want to put an end to this cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As a function of that, as a function of that, therefore - and we have heard mention of a peaceful solution, the proposal from Rambouillet, which implied the occupation of Yugoslavia - isn't that consistent with what I said a moment ago and claimed a moment ago and what you yourself are in fact saying, that peace is possible in the Balkans only under occupation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have -- Lord Ashdown, do you have any direct knowledge of this matter rather than views and opinions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Now, a relevant question or we'll bring this to a close.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that a relevant question is whether that particular thesis, which is not only Mr. Ashdown's thesis but might be a widespread one of the Balkans under occupation, is perhaps an explanation of the so-called agreement from Rambouillet, which envisaged Yugoslavia's occupation and which posed an ultimatum to Yugoslavia to accept that occupation in order to avoid war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a matter for this witness. He's not come here to give evidence about it and he hasn't done so. In due course, no doubt you can explore it with a witness who can give relevant evidence. I said that you would have one hour. You've now had it, and this examination is brought to an end. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not the first time that you have cut off my cross-examination, so I'm not really affected by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, I want to go into some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please, for Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, I want to go into some particular detail about your visit of the 23rd of June, 1998, when you were on the Albanian side of the border, and you'll recollect your evidence that that was the day you saw arms on the Albanian side and you were accompanied by someone who was a member of the Albanian police.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood him to be a member of the Albanian police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, dear, Mr. Kay. I don't believe he was, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can help you, I know that there's a statement that you gave more lately to the Tribunal, dated the 18th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't think Your Honours have a copy of that, do you? Perhaps the Prosecution would be so kind as to supply one to each of the Judges and Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It would presumably have been taken from your own sources, Lord Ashdown.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm looking at page 2 of the statement, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I can see the point you're making entirely and I can only say to you that my memory must be playing me false if it is the case that I said in this witness statement that I believe that Mr. Cengi was dressed in a uniform and insignia of the Albanian police. I can only say that I believe that must have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just want to explore the issues about that particular visit. It refers -- this passage of the statement refers to an earlier statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The date we're concerned with is the 23rd of June, 1998, if the Court want to cross-reference this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You're on the Albanian side of the border. You refer to this man in the statement as being Chief of Police.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe he was, though I can't be absolutely certain. It was a very small and rather chaotic area. He was described to me, if I recall, as Chief of Police, but it would mean the chief of the police of a very small police station in Bajram Curri.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were uncertain whether he was a member of the border police or regular police or special police.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just draw your attention, if I may, to the phrase that I constantly use: "I believe" and "I think," et cetera, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So there was an uncertainty about you as to exactly what his role as a policeman was?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I'd say I was uncertain about what his duties may have been, but I'm absolutely certain of the fact that whatever his defined duties, he had neither the numbers nor the materials - that is, vehicles, radios, et cetera - to carry out those duties effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You had met this particular person, had you, in Tirana?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not to be confused with Mr. Neritan Ceku, who was the person who I believe was either at that time or had been previously a Minister of the Interior. He was the person who organised this visit at my request, and he was the person who introduced to me to the local, as it's referred to here, police chief, Milaim Cengi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you met this man at the place you were, near the border?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Bajram Curri.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. And you believed that he was carrying a sidearm. That's your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. This is some time ago and this is my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's in your statement here and we accept the qualification. He had other policemen with him, did he?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this occasion. There were some other policemen back at the police station. Dear, I'm trying to recall. Two or three perhaps. But he was the one who came with me. I subsequently learned that he was, in fact, asked by Mr. Neritan Ceku to act as my bodyguard in this matter. This was regarded as a very dangerous area, and I had insisted, contrary to Mr. Ceku's recommendation, that rather than simply flying in and out in the same day, I should spend at least 24 hours in the area, including spending the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the statement says Mr. Cengi was accompanied by other members of, I believe, Albanian border police units, was that a group that he was with and you were with?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a group that he was accompanied with at the police station, but when we went up to the border, I drove up with the -- as I recall, with the ECMM, the European Community Monitoring Mission, in their LandRover, and he came along with them as, as I later understood, a bodyguard for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You've said that this was a lawless area. What other police presence was there at the time other than that you've told this Court?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost none. I mean, to give you an example, whilst the arms traffickers were driving around in four-wheeled vehicles, lorries, I think the police had available to them one broken-down, dilapidated, as I recall it, Yugoslav car, which was incapable of even getting to the edge of the town. They had no radio at all and they were seeking to control an area whose border frontage must have been 30 or 40 miles, with a detachment of, as I recall it, not much more than eight to ten people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The summary of your evidence was that this appeared to be a cross-border shopping place for members of the KLA, or whomsoever, whatever group, to go and purchase arms?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just want to go into that a little bit more. You referred in this statement to observing a truck heavily laden with arms. First of all, can you give a description of the truck so we've got that in mind?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't. The tracks in this area are indescribably bad. The truck, as I recall it, was a flat-bed truck, non-military in its appearance, bumping and grinding along a road with very deep potholes, considerable gradients, a dirt track. Slung over it was a tarpaulin, and as we came up behind it, the tarpaulin blew to one side and I could see boxes which I would recognise as containing small arms or small-arms ammunition piled in the back. The truck was very heavily laden. I cannot, I fear, tell you who was driving it. It was covered in a cloud of dust at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was going in which direction?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was going from Bajram Curri towards Tropoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So towards Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Tropoje, closer to the Kosovo border. Perhaps I should explain that this is an area dominated by the Berisha clan, Sali Berisha, the ex-Prime Minister of Albanian. He has a very large farmhouse in this area -- sorry. I'll slow down. In this area of Albania, when you say "farmhouse," you mean small fortress. And it was widely rumoured, though I can't prove it, that that was the centre of what was basically an international criminal drugs-trading - sorry - arms-trading centre, based on or around this farmhouse, and particularly in the village of Tropoje, towards which this truck was heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The truck itself, from your description, wasn't a military truck. It seemed to have been a private truck. And you've mentioned four-wheel-drive vehicles circulating in the area.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you went into Bajram Curri town, you would find all sorts of vehicles and all sorts of extraordinary characters. It was like a Wild West town. I didn't see four-wheeled trucks, as I recall, making the same journey we made, but I have no doubt they did or that they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And presumably, from your perspective at this time, the area of conflict where the majority of fighting was going on wasn't on the Albanian side, but it was over in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Entirely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that led to your conclusion that these arms were part of the Kosovo conflict at the time.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In dealing with the precise weapons in the back, you've referred to boxes that you recognised as containing boxes of small arms. By that, do you mean hand-held weapons?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I mean, the -- I went -- we went into Tropoje village. I saw a number of people cleaning arms and handling arms. I saw some backpacked parties moving up the very steep mountain ridges that rise out of here to a height of 6.000 feet over the passes, and I saw, and had reported to me by the ECMM, that there were occasionally mule trains going over the top of these mountains. My estimate is that the biggest armament they could have carried over would have been around a .5 machine-gun. Anything bigger would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: All going in the direction of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All going in the direction of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And again your conclusion at the time was, and because it was consistent within the atmosphere and place where you were, that these were all destined for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. They weren't destined for Serbs from that place?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Self-evidently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely. The police officer who was there with you, he didn't stop that truck?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't have stopped that truck. He did not have the military or the police resources to do so. We went into Tropoje and I said to him, "These arms are destined for the KLA, aren't they?" And he shrugged his shoulders in a knowing way and said, "No doubt they're destined for Albanians."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it was clear nothing was going to be done about it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For that, I don't believe you should blame the police. I found them committed, desperate for the extra resources, but it was perfectly clear that they were completely -- that this was an area given over to criminality, where the writ of criminals ran, not the writ of police, and whatever the best intentions of the police on the ground, they did not have the resources to cope with the problem they were faced with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The mix of people in this area was Albanians as well as Kosovar Albanians?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predominantly Albanians. There were others there whose origins I wouldn't like to have guessed at, but they were predominantly -- the natural population of Bajram Curri would be very small, swollen at the time by many visitors from outside, not many Western observers. And there is a tension between Albanians and Kosovar Albanians. There is no particular love lost between them. So the Kosovar Albanian refugees that this small community was putting up were not entirely welcome visitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the identities or background of the groups going from this area towards Kosovo, with arms on their backs and packs, were you able to determine whether they were Albanians or Albanian Kosovars?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I think they were a mixture of Kosovar Albanians who had put up with repression and the actions taking place for a very long time, local Albanians and, I have no doubt, members of the Albanian diaspora, and probably others, soldiers of fortune.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was going to come on to that, because you mentioned outsiders, and that's been mentioned as an issue in this case. Groups from outside the particular area of this part of -- or Albania as well as Kosovo, Muslim groups you may well --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm guessing here. I'm presuming that that is the case, given that there was a polyglot mixture of people there at the time. I can't identify any particular origins of any particular people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to move on now to --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But perhaps, if your point is were there Arabs there, I must be clear that I never saw any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. Your best judgement on it was that it was a highly mixed community?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My best judgement is that those were members of -- either Albanian Kosovars, Albanians, or members of the Albanian diaspora. That is my best judgement about the majority of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The box you saw on the vehicle, was that a new box of arms, or were you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can comment on it, actually. The box, as my memory recalls it, was in reasonably pristine condition, but if you had bumped your way up the tracks of Albania to Northern Albania, something which started out as a new and pristine box could easily be in a much worse condition by the time it gets to the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's just a matter of detail that might be important on the equality of arms. I'd like to move now to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm turning to page four, Your Honours, of that same statement that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the top paragraph on page 4, and it describes the place you went to, which had been a scene of an execution of some Serbs, although you did not see the bodies.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A scene of an alleged execution, but all the evidence that I found there is consistent with that allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you were with a BBC film crew at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And the British ambassador, and the military attache of the British embassy, and my own assistant, Mr. Roger Lowry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It was just the BBC film crew I wanted to ask you about. Presumably they filmed this particular spot.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, and indeed Mr. Lowry's tape, which was also -- he was carrying a small video camera. That's also recorded this incident, and those tapes have been handed over with this evidence to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was told to you that they were Serbs, and from your evidence, are we right in thinking that this was an area of obvious interest; there was people looking at it, scrutinising it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was an area well away from any habitation. I'll tell you, if you wish, the speculation about how these executions came to place -- to take place, but they can only be speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. It's just that the actual location of it isn't really that clear.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it isn't clear, because it's in the middle of a piece of farmland, well away from -- well away from any habitation. The belief of the military attache, Colonel Crossland, who was with me, was that these were some hostages taken by a KLA group who then came under attack from the Serb or Yugoslav forces and, in their flight, hastily disposed of their hostages. That is what was believed to have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So far as any information that was given to you, were these civilian Serbs or were they policemen or military people?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of this, but certainly the impression that I got was that they were civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I want to go now to the third paragraph on page 4, when you describe going to the Podgerusa valley.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the spelling here isn't quite conformed to that on the map, but as you probably know, all place names in Kosovo have two forms: One is the Serb form and the other is the Albanian form. It's quite clearly marked on the map that we saw earlier on, and I can identify if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: North-east of Orahovac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just south of Malisevo. It's spelt, I think, on this map here, g-o-r-u-s-a, but I think you probably have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know whether I've got the right place, though. That's the point. It might assist the Court if it can be --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you follow -- I can find it for you relatively easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you pull it a little bit closer? Is that possible? I'm just trying to find Malisevo. Malisevo is here. The main road runs from Pristina to Kumerane, and we then followed the road through to Malisevo. And then this here is a backroad. All of these areas here were the subject of Yugoslav army operations --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. The interpreters cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We followed the road from Pristina -- sorry. We were returning. Is this the next day, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the 28th of September.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 28th. Very well. We left Pristina very early in the morning. We came down to Kumerane. There's a Serb checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We then came down to Malisevo. Our aim was to get into this area south of Suva Reka without using the main roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these main roads were the subject of - and the areas around them - were the subject of extensive Serb military operations, Yugoslav military operations. So we chose to take a small backtrack down through here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an unmade-up track, very bumpy. We call it the Podgerusa valley because of the name of this village here, Podgerusa. Perhaps it may help you if I were to say that in Malisevo there was a Yugoslav army unit. I think it was a Yugoslav rather than MUP. There were checkpoints here which we had to negotiate, and when we came to here, we found a KLA checkpoint, and we had to negotiate that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's what I want to ask you about. You met a KLA checkpoint. How was that set up?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was set up with -- well, what astounded me was that these people were a thousand metres apart, but I saw no sign of any battles, any exchange of fire, any sentries out, on either side, I'm bound to say. The KLA position was very rudimentary. There were soldiers there with new uniforms bearing KLA militia signs on them, carrying Kalashnikov weapons, and around the sides were really, I have to say, pathetically prepared military positions, all the signs of people who have got -- had no military training. And if it had been the Yugoslav Serb intention in the area of Malisevo to overrun this position, they could have done so terribly easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So what you've got is you've got a Serb position up the road a kilometre away, and then this KLA checkpoint which was operating as a checkpoint. Presumably it stopped you, did it?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was very early in the morning. We found some soldiers warming themselves in the sun. There was no barrier there that I could see. It had been a cold night. We stopped, and I wanted to see what their uniforms were like. We were not stopped. I mean, I have to say that of the three KLAs I described earlier, it struck me this was the village defence KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But they had weapons?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had weapons. They --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many of them in total?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we saw only three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Three soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall, three, maybe four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What I've got in this statement here is: "I saw between five and ten KLA soldiers."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point I saw only three. Between -- as we passed down the Podgerusa valley, there were a few more scattered around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at this point there were only three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From your evidence, it seems that there's a stronger Yugoslav military presence within the area further north.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean -- yes, I believe so. I mean, what we knew is that there'd been extensive operations in the Drenica region. This map is not terrifically clear, but it's sort of around this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And from what we'd seen the night before as we came up to Kumerane, we saw a column of Serb tanks moving down this road here, and we actually got entangled with them slightly as they moved up here, and our view was that they were going to reinforce the operations being conducted in the Suva Reka region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. So what we had, then, was a group of soldiers, no matter how many were poorly trained, but that they were there with rifles and were there to take part in military operations?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure, absolutely. I think they were -- their purpose there was almost certainly to provide a defence against what they believed was going to happen to them, which was the same thing that had happened in the Suva Reka region. I don't know that it ever did, but it was a light, rather pathetic defence force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You met a KLA commander, did you?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met a KLA commander on the previous night. On the previous night, coming back from Suva Reka, we first traced our way back to Pristina up the Podgerusa valley, and it was growing dark. We were concerned to get back in time. The Ambassador wanted to get back to Belgrade, and I was -- it was suggested to me that I should chat with the local KLA commander, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know his identity or anything --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- like that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He struck me as being a local man who had just been put in charge of the local defence force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he have a rifle or a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't specifically recall that he did, but it's highly likely that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The building that you saw him in, what sort of building was that?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of -- just an ordinary house. He sat in the upstairs room in complete darkness. I wasn't able to see him terribly clearly. And we had a conversation extending to about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So unless you would have known it was there or been shown it, you wouldn't have known that it was the place where the local KLA commander was?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Indeed, I don't think it was the place the local KLA commander was. He was simply brought there to meet me. I suspect his headquarters were elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If that was the day before, then, just in the context of accuracy, that would have been the 27th of September?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So just looking at your journey and just putting it into a whole, it seems that from one moment you're driving into a Serb area, where there's Serb military, then they're driving down the road in countryside and you're moving to an area where there's KLA soldiers --

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you have here is the reflection of pattern which probably applied quite extensively. There were areas, the more rural areas, where the Serbs hadn't bothered to go, there was no particular attempt to establish law, and where, I suspect, the KLA were looked on as protectors against the depredations and attacks of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning now to one other matter which is also on this page. It concerns a radio message. It's the second-to-last paragraph on page 4. It says in the statement: "I recall I heard a radio message reporting the death of a number of Serb youths. They'd been killed during a grenade attack on a bar in Pec. I'm not aware of any other details about this incident."

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm -- I should say that although it's not evident from here, this refers not to this visit but to a later visit in December. I apologise if that's not clear. In December I revisited these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Prizren area and was there when there had been a substantial KLA incursion across the Albanian border which had been caught by Yugoslav forces in an ambush, in a purely military-to-military engagement. And on the night this news broke, as I recall, the news also broke that there had been a grenade attack. It was, I think, this being December 1998, the first evidence that the KLA -- that I knew of, that the KLA had done an outrage in an urban area in Pec, and I think I'm right in saying three Serb youths were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The winter of 1998 was meant to be, so to speak, a reduction in hostilities between the parties. Is that right in the context of what we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the time when the Hill agreement, the introduction of the KVM, the KDOM, was in operation as observers. And when that agreement was announced, I said that in the absence of any armed presence to back that up, inevitably the KLA would get more active as a result of the fact that the operations of the Yugoslav government had acted as a recruiting sergeant for the KLA, and that the Yugoslav forces would seek -- would begin to undermine the peace. So you are beginning to see the re-, as it were, descent back into violence, which culminated in the massacre of Racak and, of course, the necessity for Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As far as the news about the bar in Pec was concerned, was that on a local radio or some other kind of police radio?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was on the local radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the local radio.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the subject of a series of press conferences given the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And presumably in your mind, then, was -- were the thoughts: Well, the KLA have started again.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I needed to be told that. The KLA were already beginning incursions across the border. The flaw of the Hill plan was that without NATO forces to police the ceasefire, it was bound to be eroded, and it was eroded by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Lord Ashdown, you say that as a result of your interest in Bosnia and later Kosovo, you were consulted by either one or more Prime Ministers and shouted down in the House of Commons. Over what period of time, if you can be a little more precise, did your interest in Kosovo lead to negative reaction from the government at home?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must be clear that it didn't lead to negative reaction in the case of Kosovo. I was referring to the case of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the years or year when you were drawing that sort of reaction? If you can remember. Don't guess, if you can't.

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992 to 1994 probably. When I used to stand up at Prime Minister's question time, I was often referred to as the Member of Parliament for Sarajevo because I was trying to draw the government's attention to this. By 1993 or 1994, I think most people were concluding that the action that I had been recommending was indeed going to be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions. I have one minute of administrative matters about next week's witnesses after the witness has withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please correct me if I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please correct me if I'm wrong. What is suggested by your overall evidence seems that the accused had the knowledge what had been actually happening in relation to the actions of the military or police, which has been described by you as a campaign of indiscriminate terror operated against a civilian population as a punitive attempt to drive them from their houses. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm bound to say that I cannot conclude that the accused did not have that knowledge, because the very purpose of Mr. Blair's letter was to warn about the examples that had already occurred in the Drenica region of the use of excessive force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For clarification, may I ask it this way: Do you mean that the accused came to know about such atrocities perpetuated by the Serb forces because of your information or your warning, or could you articulate more on the basis of such judgement of yours?

utterances.speaker: PADDY ASHDOWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the grounds that the international community was, as in the case of the Blair letter, warning him even before I arrived of the consequences of the use of excessive force in this nature, I must presume that he knew about it, but I wanted to make explicitly clear that from the moment I had informed him and had drawn his attention to the provisions of international law, the Geneva Convention, from that moment onwards, he could not then deny knowledge of these facts if they were to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, Lord Ashdown, to give your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is -- while the -- exhibits, I think the Statute already has a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the longer version of the diary entry needs a number. And may the witness statement, if it's to be produced, also have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement will be numbered Prosecution Exhibit 81.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the longer version of the extract has already been given the original number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It has already been exhibited, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we go, if we may, for one-minute, into private session, can I alert the Court publicly to the fact that the probabilities are that the first two sessions, at least, on Monday will be in closed session, pursuant to orders of the Chamber. May we then, with the Court's leave, have a private session to assist the accused in his preparation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 18th day of March, 2002, at 9.30 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.10 p.m.,
